Tech Report: What The Telecom Bust Taught Me About AI’s Debt Boom

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1315 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The financing of the AI buildout is shifting from equity to debt, and those who invested through the telecom bubble may recognize what that shift tends to mean.
  • There is an old story in Stephen Hawking’s “A Brief History of Time” about a scientist lecturing on the universe when a woman in the audience insists that the world rests on the back of a giant turtle.
  • Industry observers note that I think of it when I look at the AI buildout because its logic has taken the same shape.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The financing of the AI buildout is shifting from equity to debt, and those who invested through the telecom bubble may recognize what that shift tends to mean.

There is an old story in Stephen Hawking’s “A Brief History of Time” about a scientist lecturing on the universe when a woman in the audience insists that the world rests on the back of a giant turtle. Asked what the turtle stands on, she replies that it’s “turtles all the way down.” Her response is what philosophers call infinite regress — a chain of claims in which each one rests on another of the same kind and solid ground never arrives.

Industry observers note that I think of it when I look at the AI buildout because its logic has taken the same shape. Valuations support borrowing, and borrowing builds capacity. The capacity then becomes proof that the valuations were right, so each claim stands on the one beneath it.

Over the past year, more of the stack has started running on debt rather than equity, and in my experience, that crossing is the moment the telecom bubble becomes the relevant history given that debt may change how these stories end.

Until recently, the AI buildout was largely an equity-financed story, with venture investment reaching record levels.

According to recent reports, crunchbase data highlights global venture funding totaled $679 billion through the first three quarters of 2026, the highest amount ever recorded for that period. AI companies attracted $102 billion in the third quarter alone, accounting for roughly 64% of global venture funding. A record 27 companies raised rounds of $1 billion or more during the quarter, collectively accounting for about a third of that total.

Equity financing carries significant risks, but unlike debt, it generally does not impose fixed repayment obligations. When investments underperform, equity investors typically absorb losses through declining valuations, while companies may retain greater flexibility to pursue their long-term strategies.

Sources indicate that that debt is now arriving in size. Meta sold $30 billion of bonds last October in one of the largest corporate debt sales on record, then returned for $25 billion more in April, with investors reportedly demanding more compensation the second time. Amazon, Alphabet and Oracle have each borrowed tens of billions of their own, and Meta’s giant Louisiana data-center campus was financed with a record $27 billion bond raised by a joint-venture partner rather than by Meta itself. Morgan Stanley expects the massive AI and cloud companies to spend about $3 trillion on infrastructure through 2028, with only about half of it expected to come from their own cash flow. The rest has to come from somewhere, and increasingly I think that somewhere is the bond market and private credit.

I watched the earlier version of this from a front-row seat, first as a venture capitalist in the late 1990s and since then as a lender to growth-stage technology companies. Telecom borrowed staggering sums against a demand forecast that was widely repeated and rarely checked, the famous claim that internet traffic was doubling every 100 days.

It has been revealed that traffic was actually doubling about once a year, spectacular growth but a fraction of what the borrowing assumed. By 2002 the telecom sector carried roughly $1 trillion in debt, much of which the chairman of the FCC told Congress would never be repaid, and WorldCom had entered what was then the largest bankruptcy in American history.

Much of the fiber the industry laid sat dark for years and was finally put to work by buyers who paid pennies on the dollar for it in bankruptcy, through a decade of restructurings and private mergers that rebuilt entire cap tables. Some companies survived that process, and many did not.

Sources indicate that the echo that concerns me most is the demand narrative. Today’s version holds that data centers are effectively leased before they are built and that the only real mistake is building too little. That may prove correct, but it is repeated with the same uniformity the traffic forecast enjoyed in 1999, and much of it rests on projections supplied by the companies doing the building. What has changed in recent months is that investors have begun demanding an answer.

Anthropic is now public, and once companies of that scale report financial results every quarter, investors can check the demand story against audited numbers.

It has been revealed that some may argue, reasonably, that my comparison fails and that the companies doing the largest borrowing may be among the most profitable enterprises ever built, with cash flows the telecom carriers never approached. A few AI companies also appear to be reaching revenue scale faster than any businesses before them.

Sources indicate that and the internet really did change everything, just as the traffic really did arrive. All of that may be true, and none of it answers the question I think a lender has to ask, which is whether the cash arrives on the schedule the debt requires. Equity can generally wait out a wrong timeline in a way debt cannot, and when borrowed money builds capacity faster than revenue arrives to service it, in my opinion, the correction tends to come through restructurings rather than quiet markdowns.

Sources indicate that none of this is a prediction that the AI buildout must end the way telecom did. The most durable lesson of the telecom bust, in my view, concerned capital structure, which decided who was still standing when demand finally caught up with capacity, long after the technology itself had been vindicated. I have spent years arguing that growth companies fear debt more than they should, and I still believe it, but the argument has always been conditional.

Debt serves borrowers whose obligations are sized to revenue they can see and lenders who underwrite fundamentals instead of narratives, and it treats everyone else harshly. I believe the borrowing stacked beneath the AI boom will be judged by that standard. Every assumption in the stack may well hold, but what I learned the last time is that once investors begin asking what the turtles are standing on, they rarely stop until they reach something solid.

David Spreng is the founder, co-CEO and co-CIO of Runway Growth Capital. He has more than 30 years of experience as a Silicon Valley venture capitalist and growth debt lender, has been involved in the formation and development of nearly 50 technology companies, and has appeared four times on the Forbes Midas List of top venture capitalists. He co-founded Decathlon Capital Partners in 2010, served on the board of the National Venture Capital Association and has participated as a panelist at the World Economic Forum in Davos.

Freshworks alums raise $53M to take on Salesforce, HubSpot with AI-native CRM

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Dreamteam, a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.
  • According to recent reports, the funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest.
  • In a recent development, traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Dreamteam, a startup founded by former Freshworks executives, has raised $53 million to challenge Salesforce and HubSpot with its AI-native CRM, betting that AI can finally shake up a market where established players have so far proved difficult to dislodge.

According to recent reports, the funding comprises seed and Series A rounds, led by Together Fund and Accel respectively, with participation from Premji Invest. The San Francisco-based startup declined to disclose the size of each round or its valuation.

In a recent development, traditional CRMs depend on salespeople to manually record customer interactions and keep deal information up to date. That often leaves businesses with incomplete or outdated information. Dreamteam aims to eliminate much of that work by automatically capturing context from sources including emails and customer conversations. It also uses AI agents to handle tasks such as follow-ups, meeting preparation, and pipeline monitoring.

Dreamteam co-founder and CEO Anand Venkatraman (pictured above, right) told TechCrunch that he had repeatedly encountered problems with traditional CRM platforms over more than 25 years in enterprise software, including at Salesforce and Freshworks. Salespeople spent considerable time updating records, yet managers still struggled to get a reliable picture of their business. “In all these years, I have never come across an instance where I could click a button and get a forecast from the CRM,” he said.

That experience led Venkatraman to co-found Dreamteam in 2025 with Senthil Kanthaswamy (pictured above, center), who spent more than nine years at Freshworks, most recently as a product leader at Freshservice, and Ramesh Parthasarathy (pictured above, left), who previously worked on AI and platform engineering at Freshworks.

At the heart of Dreamteam’s CRM is what it calls the Organization Brain. This acts as virtual memory, pulling together information from emails, meetings, and other customer interactions to build a shared record of customer relationships. Four built-in AI agents use that information to research prospects, draft follow-up emails, flag potential risks to deals, and configure CRM workflows, with sales teams retaining control over what gets sent to customers.

Sources indicate that dreamteam has signed up more than 100 customers across 13 countries in the three months since it began actively selling its product, with most paying for the service, Venkatraman said. The startup has also replaced established CRM platforms at several businesses, including Salesforce at healthcare organization DMS Health and HubSpot at other customers.

In a recent development, the advertising sales team at media streaming tech giant Plex also chose Dreamteam over HubSpot and other AI-native CRM alternatives, Venkatraman told TechCrunch. Plex’s co-founder and chief product officer Scott Olechowski said Dreamteam’s ability to integrate with AI tools already used across the company was a “game changer.”.

Sources indicate that replacing established CRM platforms at scale may prove more difficult. In a blog post earlier this year, venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) argued that while AI could transform how businesses manage customer relationships, existing CRMs are likely to remain the systems where customer records are stored, with a fresh generation of AI-powered tools capturing much of the value by working on top of them.

Venkatraman acknowledged that Salesforce and HubSpot are unlikely to disappear anytime soon, but noted that their entrenched positions do not guarantee they will dominate the next generation of CRM software.

“We see this as an electric-car moment for systems of record,” he noted, adding that AI requires a fundamental rethink of how CRMs are built — not simply adding new features to existing platforms.

Kanthaswamy believes startups have a window of two to five years to gain ground before established CRM providers can fully adapt to AI. Rebuilding software around a fundamentally different architecture takes time, he stated, giving newer companies an opportunity to attract customers while incumbents work to overhaul their existing products.

Recent findings suggest that dreamteam also plans to expand beyond sales into other parts of the customer lifecycle, including onboarding, customer support, and upselling. The startup already has a feature called Magic Apps that allows customers to create custom applications and dashboards within the CRM using natural-language instructions, without writing code.

According to recent reports, right now, Dreamteam employs more than 35 people, with its engineering team based in Chennai and its go-to-market operations in the United States. Kanthaswamy said the startup aims to reach eight figures in annual revenue by the end of 2027, though he declined to disclose the startup’s current revenue.

At AWS, he will lead an organization that unites Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3), database and analytics services.

“MK brings deep technical roots, a customer-obsessed mindset and experience building data platforms at global scale,” Garman said in an email to staff.

Earlier in his career, MK spent more than a decade each at Oracle and Microsoft.

Scofield served as chief of staff to OpenAI’s Vijaye Raji, CTO of applications. Beltran and Echols, both software engineers, were members of the organization’s technical staff.

More recently, Brandon Zinn joined the stealth startup as head of sales. All four overlapped in earlier roles at Statsig. In a post today on LinkedIn, Zinn asked for leads with home services owners “who could use help getting more work or making the business easier to run.”.

According to recent reports, the team is working with business owners in “roofing, tree care, plumbing, HVAC, painting, etc. Especially teams of 3–15 people where a lot still falls directly on the owner,” Zinn said.

Beltran noted in a separate post that the startup has passed $100,000 in annual recurring revenue and is rapidly developing its software.

It has been revealed that — Portal Space Systems, a Bothell, Wash.-based space company, has appointed Egbert Maben as principal satellite guidance, navigation and control (GNC) engineer — the startup’s first dedicated GNC hire. Last month, Portal reached Earth orbit for the second time this year.

Recent findings suggest that maben joined from Blue Origin, where he was a leader in GNC and hardware integration and helped resolve mission-critical hardware failures. He also tackled assembly, integration and test, a process that verifies the performance of software and hardware components. He previously spent nearly two decades at Lockheed Martin.

Sources indicate that maben, the organization notes, has been keeping bees since ninth grade. “The only thing that’s left to see is whether Egbert, like bees, will be using dance to communicate those directives to our spacecraft,” Portal remarked on LinkedIn.

According to recent reports, — Seattle-based Yoodli has named Jessica Evans as its first mid-market sales leader.The startup recently expanded from helping people practice speeches, sales pitches and job interviews to providing corporate training across a wide range of skills. Evans joins from ClickUp.

— PATH, a Seattle-based global health nonprofit, has appointed three new board members:.

Recent findings suggest that — Ian McAllister joined Boston-based Toast as vice president of Product, Video AI, in October after the restaurant software company acquired Airloom AI, the Seattle-area startup he founded and led as CEO. A longtime Seattle tech GM and product leader, he spent 12 years at Amazon and also held leadership roles at Airbnb and Uber.

McAllister stated the idea for Airloom came when his wife, Sara McAllister, asked him to pick a security camera system for Allister, the Mercer Island restaurant and cocktail bar she owns and runs as GM. McAllister started Airloom AI to help restaurants use their existing video to improve the guest experience and operations. At Toast, he’ll continue that effort by combining Airloom’s technology with Toast’s platform. He’s building out Toast’s Vision AI team by hiring for multiple Seattle-based and remote product, engineering and AI/ML roles.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Revolution, the investment firm cofounded 14 years ago by entrepreneur-investor Steve Case, has closed its second Rise of the Rest seed fund with $150 million in capital commitments, just like the debut fund it announced two years ago.

Rise of the Rest — which fund startups outside of the biggest U.S. tech hubs in an effort to foster innovation and momentum elsewhere — has rounded up some of the funding from institutional investors, presumably, but also from numerous very wealthy individuals.

According to Forbes, which is currently hosting a summit where Case announced the newly introduced fund, some of the new fund’s backers include Jeff Bezos of Amazon, Sara Blakely of Spanx, hedge fund manager Ray Dalio, Under Armour cofounder Kevin Plank, former Tennessee governor Bill Haslam, and Apollo Global Management cofounder Joshua Harris.

Some of these investors backed the first fund, too, including Bezos and Dalio.

In a recent development, very notably, Hillbilly Elegy author J.D. Vance, who ran the first fund with Case, has stepped back, and longtime Revolution investor David Hall will manage the second fund instead.

According to recent reports, certainly, that first fund kept its investors busy, with stakes in 125 companies. Barely a week passes without a startup announcing some funding from the Rise of the Rest team.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that it’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S.
  • Our Next Energy (ONE) had some close calls, but soon it will go public via SPAC, the tech giant exclusively told TechCrunch.
  • ONE notes it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that it’s never been easy to run a battery startup in the U.S. There have been more failures than successes over the last 20 years, and whipsawing federal policy has caused more than a few battery companies to shut shop.

Not all of them die, though. Our Next Energy (ONE) had some close calls, but soon it will go public via SPAC, the tech giant exclusively told TechCrunch.

ONE notes it is valued at $600 million pre-money, and it expects the merger with Wen Acquisition Corp. will bring $400 million in gross proceeds assuming no redemptions. The combined organization will trade on the Nasdaq under the ticker “ONEE,” and the pro forma implied equity value is $1 billion.

Over the years, ONE has raised $483 million, according to PitchBook, and at one point was valued at $1.3 billion. It has also received tens of millions of dollars in incentives tied to investments and job creation in Michigan.

Recent findings suggest that ONE is the brainchild of former Ford and Apple engineer Mujeeb Ijaz, who designed a way for electric vehicles to draw power from two batteries of different chemistries. In ONE’s first setup, it paired lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) and with a manganese-rich chemistry, which would let each chemistry play to its strengths: LFP could be used day in, day out, while the more fragile but energy-dense, manganese-rich one would work for long, infrequent road trips. An initial prototype traveled over 600 miles on a single charge.

But the EV market didn’t take off as quickly as anticipated, and automakers wanted to buy at lower prices (usually from China). Both of those reasons helped sink ONE’s first attempt at a Series C in late 2023. The startup had to lay off a chunk of its staff, and eventually vacated its lease for a planned $1.6 billion factory in Michigan.

The rough patch led to Ijaz’s ouster as CEO in December 2023, only to have him return to the position in March 2025 after a new round of funding closed. (His brother’s investment firm co-led the round.).

Sources indicate that part of the critique aimed at ONE during Ijaz’s first tenure as CEO was that the manufacturer spent too much time developing new products instead of focusing on one or two, as most startups tend to do. When Ijaz came back to the helm last year, he noted that ONE would leave the automotive market and focus on grid-scale batteries.

ONE isn’t alone in pivoting away from vehicle batteries. American automakers, which had similarly rosy views of EV adoption, also bet significant on battery factories and supply chains. When sales didn’t pop in the U.S. like they have in China or Europe, they had to find an outlet for that capacity, and the grid started looking like the obvious target once it started groaning under the weight of AI data centers. Both Ford and GM have announced their own energy storage products.

Many latest grid-scale batteries use LFP, which is safer and cheaper than those used in most EVs in the U.S., and Ijaz saw an opportunity for ONE there as well. “We go back to the origins of LFP in this country and even to some of the factories that are in China,” he mentioned. Indeed, just over a decade ago Ijaz led the automotive division at A123 Systems, the organization that first commercialized the chemistry.

Soon, Ijaz saw other opportunities for ONE’s batteries, including defense and locomotives.

The defense play isn’t surprising. Nearly every battery organization I talk with these days mentions defense, in part because it’s a market that Chinese companies can’t play in. Building an American supply chain means that a company can sell batteries at a premium, shielded as they are from Chinese competition. It’s a higher-margin market, though much smaller than EVs.

According to recent reports, my recent conversation with Ijaz last week was the first time I’d heard a organization pitch rail companies as potential customers, though. Ijaz noted ONE is “finding a lot of traction in” that market. The company has built a hybrid locomotive that uses a 2.8 megawatt-hour battery, and another he calls a micro-hybrid, which uses a smaller battery to start the diesel engine faster, similar to a stop-start system on a fossil fuel car or truck.

“Our customers are seeing a 50% improvement in diesel fuel consumption, which is a major deal,” Ijaz said.

Recent findings suggest that right now, ONE has three business lines, which could be a sign of its old culture creeping back into the picture. But Ijaz said the addition of defense and rail were driven by the bottom line: Grid-scale battery customers are also “very much like automotive customers, where they were willing to buy from China as long as the price was low enough,” he said.

“Believe me, I would have loved to have made that grid business into the single business of the company. But the customers would look and then be taken away to a Chinese option because of the pricing, and the tariffs also leading them to that conclusion,” Ijaz said. “And so we decided that we needed a more durable market, and we looked for who in the customer base valued an American battery company.”.

Recent findings suggest that today, ONE operates a pack assembly plant in Novi, Michigan, which can put together packs from cells at a rate of 3 gigawatt-hours per year. The plant uses cells from China-based and non-China-based suppliers, as well as ONE’s own cells from a smaller factory nearby, which is right now being upgraded to make 50 megawatt-hours of batteries per year.

In its investor pitch, which TechCrunch has reviewed, ONE distills its business lines into defense and rail. Drones and submarines make up the majority of what ONE sees as a $16.2 billion market. Defense-focused data centers get lumped in there, too, contributing $4.1 billion to the defense business. (That appears to be the main outlet for grid-scale batteries.) The other line, which serves the rail industry, is expected to be worth $28.2 billion.

Recent findings suggest that both markets are sizable, but they pale in comparison to the EV sector, which is worth about $73 billion today, and could grow to $200 billion by the end of the decade, according to Grand View Research. This year, ONE expects to bring in $30 million in revenue, and hopes to make double that next year. The company said it has $200 million in binding, multi-year contracts with railroads and defense contractors.

Sources indicate that ONE hasn’t closed the door on the automotive industry, Ijaz said. “Automotive still is a race to the bottom on margins,” he said. “As time goes on, if we win an automotive contract for any purpose, we’ll take a look at it, but not at any cost.”.

ONE’s pitch centers on the so-called foreign entity of concern (FEOC) restrictions: The U.S. government can’t buy batteries made in China or those made using minerals from China-controlled supply chains, so ONE will target them first.

Sources indicate that but it’s a pitch that many battery companies are making today. Whether investors buy into ONE’s vision will depend on if they think the tech giant has parted with its tumultuous past and found a focus. It will need both to succeed in the increasingly cutthroat battery industry.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Grace Kaste on Nov 23, 2026 at 3:29 pmNovember 23, 2026 at 3:29 pm.
  • Recent advancements in AI have cast a cloud over college students studying software engineering.
  • But at CSEED’s Buildspace Demo Day last week, 60 undergraduates in the University of Washington student club showed that AI hasn’t dampened their drive to create.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Grace Kaste on Nov 23, 2026 at 3:29 pmNovember 23, 2026 at 3:29 pm.

Recent advancements in AI have cast a cloud over college students studying software engineering. Jobs seem to be disappearing every day, while coursework can be done by chatbots.

But at CSEED’s Buildspace Demo Day last week, 60 undergraduates in the University of Washington student club showed that AI hasn’t dampened their drive to create. If anything, it’s allowing them to build things they wouldn’t have been able to before.

Sources indicate that “We’re seeing projects that normal college students would not be expected to make,” club co-president Leonard Paya mentioned. “As AI becomes more advanced, you can see how fast they scale up their knowledge and execute on things that are truly amazing.”.

In a recent development, CSEED, founded a few years ago and already one of UW’s largest clubs, supports aspiring software designers and engineers. It’s funded by the Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering, as well as venture capital firms such as AI House, Madrona and Pack Ventures. Its members have gone on to join startup incubators including Y Combinator, Z Fellows and Founders Inc.

Sources indicate that twice a year, CSEED accepts applications for its Buildspace cohort, a program for students with hardware, software or design pitches. Over six weeks, the cohort meets up for build sessions, and they also receive mentorship, supplies and AI credits. Demo Day on Nov. 17 at the UW’s Gates Center marked the conclusion of the sixth Buildspace cohort, with 30 inventions presented to 150 audience members.

In a recent development, “We’ve brought together curious and ambitious students from all backgrounds,” vice president Amy Lu mentioned. “CSEED gives them the community to turn their ideas into reality.”.

One of the most technically advanced ideas presented was DubDash, a fully autonomous robot for delivering food orders from the dining hall to dorms.

“The best part of this is that these people were all freshmen who hadn’t yet taken robotics classes,” Paya said. “Who would have thought that four freshmen could make a fully fledged robot in six weeks?”.

Recent findings suggest that according to junior and Buildspace co-director Talal Kheiry, that’s a testament to AI. Buildspace members receive AI credits, which Kheiry noted have changed everything.

“AI helps guide them through the gritty parts of the project, so they can just focus on the creative parts without worrying about the technical stuff,” Kheiry mentioned.

Other inventions offered a glimpse into what’s on students’ minds these days. From notification-silencing focus apps to social connectors and mental health education platforms, nearly half of them had to do with curbing the effects of social media.

Industry observers note that “Social media isn’t social anymore,” Junaid Akhtar told the audience as he and his three team members presented. “It’s just a place to see media. Our goal is to make social media bring people together again.”.

His team’s presentation was the audience’s favorite: a satirical pitch for a platform they call FeedPicks, which creates live ranked prediction markets of friends’ social media feeds. Their demo won an award for “best energy” at the end of the night.

It has been revealed that other inventions sought to get users off their screens altogether. Joe Chae, a freshman at the Allen School, presented Pidgin, a Tinder-style app that helps users who want to practice each other’s languages to meet up in real life.

Industry observers note that “I came to UW hoping to meet some Korean international students here and learn to speak Korean with my relatives, but I didn’t meet anyone,” Chae said. “So I thought, what if I made an app that could help me find someone who speaks Korean natively and wants to learn English?”.

Also focused on the real world was Sasha Bogatirev’s Hadden Cybernetics. Bogatirev built a wearable gaming console that takes in information from a user’s environment and turns it into a game.

In a recent development, “The person has to pay attention to their surroundings,” Bogatirev remarked. “The idea is to prompt the imagination as much as possible for someone to experience another world.”.

His prototype used the ESP32-S3 microcontroller to render the visuals onto wearable glasses. An nRF chip on the wristband takes in scripted gestures, which he trained to turn a player’s gestures into shields, lightning strikes and fireballs. Next, he prepares to add haptics using hardware supplied by CSEED.

According to recent reports, andrew Edwards also built a video game accessory: cStar, which is an open source, low-cost console that can play a game on any TV screen by loading it onto an SD card and popping it into a 3D-printed box. Inside that box is a microcontroller like you’d find inside a stopwatch or a microwave, unlike the highly complicated circuitry used by an Xbox or PlayStation.

Industry observers note that “We were able to squeeze HDMI video out of the microcontroller, which allows us to show 2D and 3D graphics on a home television set,” Edwards said. “Since the games are based on standard SD cards, a curious programmer can just write software on the computer, stick it onto an SD card, put it in the console and you’re ready to play.”.

Other notable inventions presented at Demo Day:.

This cohort was their largest and most competitive yet. Next up, under the guidance of club advisor and Allen School professor Kurtis Heimerl, CSEED is looking to expand. They’ve started hosting build sessions every Saturday that are open to non-students.

In a recent development, to do that, they’ll need to fundraise. According to CSEED co-president Benya Vahdat, they’ve already used up their Allen School allotment for the year, and they’re now in the process of raising money from donors. They recently incorporated as CSEED Foundation and received nonprofit status in Washington state.

“We want to grow this mentality of building, and maybe expand across campuses not just in Washington but across the country,” Vahdat noted. “Maybe even globally.”.

The daily chart of XRP has yielded a death cross, the first time the signal has popped up in 2026. XRP experienced a death cross on its daily chart in November 2025 and then entered a downtrend for several months before a recovery in August 2026.

Buoyed by optimism around favorable crypto regulation, XRP had already seen a golden cross in September 2026 before this. But that didn’t last long. The Senate stalled on the Clarity Act, a bill on crypto market structure.

Since then, the wider crypto market has struggled. The declines deepened in late October, as concerns over artificial intelligence valuations and spending fueled a broad tech sell-off. They were compounded by the $6.3 billion Binance hack and weakening institutional ETF demand.

U.S. spot XRP ETFs recorded about $4.97 million in net outflows Friday, according to SoSoValue data, with the withdrawals concentrated in Bitwise's XRP fund.

Throughout November, the crypto market has struggled due to a combination of dollar strength and leveraged liquidations.

The 50 DMA fell below the 200 DMA on the daily chart, completing a death cross pattern, coinciding with a sharp decline that took XRP below a key support and left leveraged traders nursing heavy losses.

As seen on the monthly chart, XRP has declined below the monthly 50 MA, a key level that supported its 500% rise in November 2024.

Sources indicate that however, all hope is not lost as the token’s daily relative strength index has dropped below 30, a level generally considered oversold. That can accompany a short-term rebound, but it does not fully establish that the decline has ended.

In a recent discussion on CNBC, Ripple CEO Brad Garlinghouse expressed hope for a crypto rebound.

Garlinghouse stated that the recent crypto sell-off reflects investors shifting funds into high-profile IPOs such as Anthropic. He expects to see the crypto markets bounce back after the listing, pointing to a similar rally after SpaceX’s IPO. If this scenario plays out, XRP will look to return to $1 and then $1.2. In contrast, support remains at $0.77 if the ongoing sell-off continues.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chan Park feels like “an eternal nomad.” He has since age 12, when he moved from Korea to the U.S., where he attended middle school in Minnesota, followed by high school in New Jersey, followed by college in New Hampshire. Then he really began to bounce around. Park worked as a trader in New York out of college, embraced the ski-bum life in Utah, then headed to Asia for Uber, where he spent six years, running its expansion team, then managing its entire Southeast Asia business out of Singapore.

More specifically, he was responsible for eight countries across the region, and 350 people, which didn’t give him a lot of time to organize his home. But he wasn’t overwhelmed by the chaos. Instead, he claims that in Singapore, something unusual happened. “There’s this huge culture of landlords furnishing space to attract expats,” explains Park. “The furnishings aren’t super high-end, but they’re well-designed and well put together, and it enabled me to be basically moved in as soon as I put my clothes in the closet.” Suddenly, coming home was a treat — a latest sensation for him. “For the first time, I was proud to host friends for dinners and barbecues and to just open the door and relax.”.

Park knew his U.S. friends could benefit from the same experience, and before long, he was talking with his Dartmouth classmate turned product and industrial designer Christian Talmage about forming their own company. Enter Oliver Space, which provides a lot of what that Singaporean landlord delivered to Park. It furnishes places for busy professionals, making moving into a fresh home as easy as hanging up their clothes.

Industry observers note that the now year-old service is available in the Bay Area only. And Oliver Space employs just a dozen people so far. But the organization has already gained enough traction to attract $6.8 million in seed funding from an interesting array of investors, including Mayfield, Abstract Ventures, investors Jana Messerschmidt and April Underwood, Opendoor founder Eric Wu, and Kevin and Julia Hartz of Eventbrite, among others.

Now, Oliver Space just has to grow as rapidly, or more so, than other furniture-as-service startups to recently attract funding.

Breaking: Nanbeige4.3-33B Ties Qwen3.8-27B on Intelligence Index, but Spends 44% More Output Tokens

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1103 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nanbeige4.3-33B matches Qwen3.8-27B at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but uses 158K output tokens per task against 110K.
  • According to recent reports, two models just posted the same score.
  • According to recent reports, nanbeige4.3-33B, a dense 33-billion-parameter reasoning model from the foundation model team at BOSS Zhipin, scores 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Nanbeige4.3-33B matches Qwen3.8-27B at 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index but uses 158K output tokens per task against 110K. Here is what that costs locally.

According to recent reports, two models just posted the same score. One needed 158,000 output tokens per task to get there. The other needed 110,000.

According to recent reports, nanbeige4.3-33B, a dense 33-billion-parameter reasoning model from the foundation model team at BOSS Zhipin, scores 20 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index v5. According to Artificial Analysis's evaluation, published November 5, that matches Qwen3.8 27B at its xhigh reasoning setting. The model is open weights under Apache 2.0, accepts text only, and has a 524K-token context window.

In a recent development, behind the tie sits a gap in effort. Artificial Analysis says Nanbeige used 158K output tokens per Intelligence Index task against 110K for Qwen3.8 27B, about 44% more. That weighted average covers answer and reasoning tokens across all nine v5 evaluations, including agentic tool-use turns. For anyone running these models, tokens translate into time, electricity or money, so the same score doesn't mean the same cost.

It has been revealed that the Intelligence Index v5 combines nine evaluations, among them AA-Briefcase, AutomationBench-AA, Terminal-Bench 4.0, FrontierCode 2.0 and AA-Omniscience. A score of 20 puts Nanbeige well above the 6 of Muse Glimmer, a 30B model in the same comparison. Artificial Analysis also notes that Nanbeige sets a latest Pareto-optimal point for Intelligence Index against total parameters, since both it and Qwen3.8 27B are dense models. A larger mixture-of-experts model like DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, by contrast, scores 33 while activating only 16B parameters per token.

Industry observers note that the model card Nanbeige's lab published on Hugging Face describes the base model, positioned as the flagship teacher for the Nanbeige4.3 series. The lab indicates it will distill agentic capabilities into smaller models, such as an upcoming 3B version. On base-model benchmarks, the card highlights 66.9 on MMLU-Pro against 59.3 for Gemma4-31B-Base. Those figures belong to the base model and are separate from the reasoning model's Intelligence Index result.

In a recent development, the two models reach 20 by different routes. Nanbeige scores 30% on Terminal-Bench 4.0 against 6% for Qwen, and 16% on the CritPt v2 Hard Subset against 4%. It also edges Qwen on AutomationBench-AA, 53% to 48%.

Recent findings suggest that elsewhere, it falls behind. On AA-Briefcase v1.1 it scores 1162 Elo against 1391, on FrontierCode 2.0 11% against 15%, and on HLE-Diamond 7% against 15%. The knowledge test tells the most distinctive story. On AA-Omniscience v1.1, Nanbeige scores -4 against Qwen's -6, with an 18% hallucination rate against 29%. Yet it answers only 29% of questions against 43%, declines 71% of them and gets 12% correct against 17%.

For general question answering, Qwen's higher accuracy is the better result.

In a recent development, output tokens aren't a vanity metric. A reasoning model writes out its thinking as tokens, and every one costs decode time. If both models ran at the same speed on the same hardware, Nanbeige would take about 44% longer to finish a typical task.

Recent findings suggest that local decoding adds a second factor. Generation is usually limited by memory bandwidth, because each latest token requires reading the model's weights, and a 33B dense model reads about 20% more weight data per token than a 27B dense model. Assuming the same quantization and the same memory-bound hardware, those two effects compound to roughly 1.7 times the wall-clock time per task. That figure is a back-of-the-envelope calculation, not a measured result.

Nor is there a hosted alternative to soften the blow. Artificial Analysis lists no confirmed public first-party or third-party APIs for Nanbeige, so unlike Qwen, which is sold per token through Alibaba's API, the cost is the hardware you run it on and the time it takes.

According to recent reports, artificial Analysis describes the model as small enough to run locally on a laptop, which holds true with a caveat. The weights are published in BF16, which at 33 billion parameters means roughly 66 GB, far beyond almost any laptop. At 8-bit, the weights fall to about 33 GB, and at 4-bit to about 17 GB, plus memory for the context cache. A machine with 24 GB of unified memory or more can plausibly hold a 4-bit build, though a long context will push it.

Recent findings suggest that the vendor's own quickstart points the other way. The card's SGLang and vLLM examples both set tensor parallelism across four GPUs, which suggests the reference deployment is a multi-GPU server. Its Transformers example also enables trust_remote_code=True, which runs code from the repository. Reading that code first is the safer move, as is serving the model through vLLM or SGLang instead.

Sources indicate that quantization changes the model, too. The Intelligence Index numbers come from Artificial Analysis's own runs, so a 4-bit local build may score somewhat lower, or generate different token counts, than the version they evaluated.

It has been revealed that this release is a clean example of why a headline score isn't enough. Nanbeige delivers Qwen-level results at 33B, with strengths in terminal tasks and physics reasoning and a more cautious answering style. The price for those strengths is length.

In a recent development, anyone choosing between the two should run both on their own workload and record three numbers: the score on their tasks, output tokens per task and seconds per task on their hardware. For terminal-heavy, agentic work, Nanbeige's profile may justify the longer runs. For knowledge-heavy or latency-sensitive work, Qwen's shorter, more accurate answers look stronger.

Three signals are worth watching next: whether the 3B distilled version keeps the model's strengths, whether other labs report the same token behavior, and whether anyone publishes quantized local benchmarks. Until then, the simplest summary is also the most accurate: same score, different bill.

Island is a new screen-time app that turns staying off your phone into a game

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (923 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time.
  • This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Databricks, and Microsoft.
  • Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new startup is taking a different approach to helping people manage their screen time. Instead of blocking apps or restricting the phone’s use after a set period, an app called Island encourages you to meet your screen time goals by way of a farming simulator game. Yes, a game! Island works by rewarding you when you’re disciplined enough to meet your goals with a “credit score” that increases your farm’s production, unlocking new crops, animals, and other content.

This carrot-instead-of-stick approach was dreamed up by entrepreneurs Ashish Selvaraj (CEO) and Ethan Pronev (CTO), who met while studying at the University of Waterloo, then went on to work at companies that included Jane Street, Citadel Securities, Databricks, and Microsoft.

Later, they quit their jobs to join the startup accelerator Y Combinator, where they first tried out other ideas in areas like B2B and software-as-a-service, but weren’t finding the right fit.

Island ended up being their fifth pivot, and the first the founders actually found themselves enjoying.

“Once we were in YC, I think there’s a big mindset — I think in [San Francisco], in general — of, ‘selling shovels.’ Everyone wants to ‘sell shovels’ to other companies, and around us, that’s just what was going on,” explains Selvaraj, speaking about the concept that many successful startups sell the tools, infrastructure, or services to others following whatever the current market boom or trend may be.

Industry observers note that “So all the ideas we had — we tried these things — but we found that we weren’t passionate about it. Like idea after idea seemed like ultimately the product was just a dashboard with some kind of different backend,” he added. “It felt like we quit our jobs … just to do something that was a variation of that.”.

With Island, the team gets to tap into their creativity, having drawn the pixel art themselves.

It has been revealed that “A lot of people do use [AI] models to generate the art, but we felt that it had a certain character when we drew it ourselves,” he told TechCrunch. “I feel like with Claude getting so good, there’s a tendency to give away every task to Claude. But ultimately it feels like there’s something else that comes out when you do it yourself, especially in something like art,” Selvaraj said.

Sources indicate that what’s more, the app does appear to be successful in helping consumers meet their goals, the startup’s early data shows. After early testing and an October launch, the team states that the majority of its users (82%) will end their screen time right at the limit they’ve set. Many more are ending their screen time when they get the “15 minutes left” warning.

Sources indicate that island could appeal to those who have given up on other screen time apps out of frustration because the app doesn’t actually lock you out of apps or your phone. That’s something that can end up being more disruptive, especially when you’re in the middle of doing something, like posting, sharing, commenting, or chatting, among other things. Instead, Island taps into users’ own self-discipline and their desire to see their island flourish to encourage screen time breaks.

The idea to encourage consumers to keep their goals by offering some other type of in-app reward system isn’t entirely novel. Last year, Hank Green’s screen time app Focus Friend went viral for its experience, which involved a little friend that could only knit items that, in turn, allowed you to get points used to decorate your room when you were focused on your non-distracting apps.

In a recent development, similar ideas have been used in self-care apps and habit-trackers like Finch, Amaru, Belly, Flora, Urso, and others. But Island expands this concept from being focused on helping out a virtual friend or pet to one that’s more of a game — and one where you can experience the consequences without “having to torture your pet,” notes Selvaraj.

Island also allows users to add friends and visit each other’s islands, compete in group challenges, and keep each other accountable by tying your island together with one friend of your choosing. In the latter scenario, if either friend goes over their limit, both of their islands will suffer.

The startup indicates Island has proven to be fairly “sticky” with a 51% daily active people-to-monthly active users ratio, and a day 30 retention rate of 49%, meaning 49% of users were still active on the app on the 30th day since the app was installed.

The app is right now free to use, with a $39.99 per year subscription that allows you to set individual limits on different apps, instead of just an overall daily screen time limit. The company hasn’t raised additional seed funding outside of YC, but plans to begin marketing the app on social media for the rest of the year.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 24, 2026 at 6:44 amNovember 24, 2026 at 6:44 am.
  • It has been revealed that many Microsoft business customers are still wading through the session slide decks and “Book of News” collection of product and strategy announcements from Microsoft’s Ignite confab last week.
  • According to recent reports, microsoft’s curated Ignite keynote and session spotlights were, unsurprisingly, dedicated to Microsoft AI in all its guises — Copilot, the Microsoft IQ intelligence platforms and Agent 365.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Mary Jo Foley on Nov 24, 2026 at 6:44 amNovember 24, 2026 at 6:44 am.

It has been revealed that many Microsoft business customers are still wading through the session slide decks and “Book of News” collection of product and strategy announcements from Microsoft’s Ignite confab last week. But not all the upcoming goodies announced there (or simultaneous with this year’s Microsoft Ignite show, which kicked off Nov. 17) might have made it onto everyone’s radar.

According to recent reports, microsoft’s curated Ignite keynote and session spotlights were, unsurprisingly, dedicated to Microsoft AI in all its guises — Copilot, the Microsoft IQ intelligence platforms and Agent 365. But there was some other important news last week that Microsoft customers could find equally, if not more, interesting and useful.

Among my picks for the “make sure you didn’t miss this” list:.

Copilot without the M365 subscription prerequisite arrives next week: Despite a LOT of talk about Copilot, “a new OS for work,” Microsoft didn’t mention anything at all during Ignite about a new purchasing option for Copilot that is set to go live on Dec. 1. Starting then, Microsoft will offer a version of Copilot to small business and enterprise customers without the current prerequisite of having a certain paid Microsoft 365 initiative.

For a flat fee of $21 per user per month for small businesses and $30 per user per month for enterprise customers (before discounts), people will be able to buy this fresh standalone Copilot offering, as Microsoft quietly unveiled back in October on its Partner Center site.

Currently, to buy Copilot, business customers need to have purchased a qualifying Microsoft 365 subscription plan before they shell out even more money for Copilot. Because of this requirement, Microsoft isn’t competitive price-wise when pitted against OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude entry-level business tiers.

The latest offer is for new customers buying through any of Microsoft’s channels, including its Cloud Solution Provider program, across commercial, education, government and nonprofit sectors.

I’ve got a lot of questions about this new offer, including where Copilot chats are stored and how/if customers will get some kind of access to the Microsoft IQ technology that underlies Copilot and is positioned as its secret sauce if they don’t have a Microsoft 365 subscription. I’ve asked Microsoft, but no word back so far.

Azure Linux 4.0 is now ready for prime time: Revealed on the same day Ignite kicked off (but without a mention during the conference), Microsoft’s own commercial Linux distribution, Azure Linux 4.0, is now generally available.

According to recent reports, the 4.0 release is interesting for a few reasons. First, it is the first release of Azure Linux — formerly known as Common Base Linux (CBL)-Mariner — designed as a general-purpose server OS for customer virtual machines, and it is based on the Fedora Linux stack. Checking off the requisite AI box, Azure Linux 4.0 is “purpose-built for cloud native and AI workloads,” as Microsoft said back in May.

It has been revealed that microsoft officials have noted two-thirds of customer cores in Azure run Linux (not Windows Server). Microsoft has acknowledged the platforms running Microsoft 365, GitHub and OpenAI’s ChatGPT “all sit on Linux foundations.”.

Microsoft has supported a wide variety of Linux distributions on Azure for years but never made its own available for commercial use by customers and partners until now.

Windows Server 2028 is in the works: Yes, another on-premises version of Windows Server is coming. Christened Windows Server 2028, the next release, likely to debut in late 2027, is now in public preview.

Microsoft mentioned Server 2028 in its Book of News and in passing in some sessions, but it was not positioned as a top-tier announcement.

The 2028 release includes some expected and a few surprise features, such as making 32-bit app support an optional component rather than installing it by default. That change, along with a hardened Server Core configuration included by default, is designed to improve the security of the platform from the get-go. But they may present potential backward-compatibility risks.

Industry observers note that microsoft is positioning Server 2028 similarly to the way it has been pushing Windows client lately: as a way to run AI workloads more cheaply because they can run locally. The “unmetered intelligence” pitch strikes again.

Sure, Microsoft can’t make every announcement a centerpiece in a two-plus-hour (waah!) opening keynote. But sometimes, hidden gems deserve their moments in the sun. Or pouring rain ….

5 Interesting Startup Deals You May Have Missed: Reflecting Sunlight From Space, Better Breathing And Smarter Garbage Trucks

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1544 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Crunchbase

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar.
  • What if solar farms could keep generating electricity after sunset with a little help from mirrors orbiting Earth?
  • According to recent reports, those are two of the more unusual ideas that attracted startup investment in the past month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a monthly column that runs down five interesting startup funding deals that may have flown under the radar. Check out our previous entry here.

What if solar farms could keep generating electricity after sunset with a little help from mirrors orbiting Earth? Or researchers could send an experiment into space for less than the price of a car?

According to recent reports, those are two of the more unusual ideas that attracted startup investment in the past month. Our latest roundup also includes a company bringing AI to the old-school business of garbage hauling, another rethinking how factories are programmed, and a consumer brand betting that better breathing could become a big business. Let’s take a closer look.

Solar power has one rather obvious limitation: The sun goes down.

To that end, Reflect Orbital is working on a solution that sounds straight out of science fiction. The Hawthorne, California-based startup wants to put giant mirrors in orbit to redirect sunlight toward specific locations on Earth, potentially allowing solar farms to keep generating electricity longer after sunset.

It has been revealed that the tech giant recently declared $73.5 million in new funding, bringing its total funding to more than $102 million, per Crunchbase. Existing investors Sequoia Capital, Lux Capital and Starship Ventures participated, alongside new backers including Buckley Ventures, Convective Capital, The Uncommon Group and Salesforce Ventures 1.

Reflect Orbital is developing lightweight, foldable reflectors that it says can be released aboard satellites and deployed in low Earth orbit. The manufacturer envisions using them not only to extend solar power generation, but also to illuminate disaster zones for nighttime search-and-rescue operations or construction sites after dark.

Industry observers note that the idea remains unproven in orbit, however. Reflect Orbital is targeting the second quarter of 2027 for its first demonstration mission, which has received FCC approval. The funding will help support those initial launches, further development of its reflector technology, and commercial partnerships.

The raise comes during a record year for space technology funding. By late August, investors had poured $20.3 billion into space- and satellite-related startups globally, per Crunchbase data, already comfortably exceeding previous annual records.

Nasal strips have been around for decades, but Intake Breathing Technology thinks there’s room for a serious upgrade.

The Santa Barbara, California-based consumer wellness manufacturer recently declared a $62 million investment from Camino Partners, the investment platform founded by KIND Snacks entrepreneur Daniel Lubetzky.

Intake makes a patented magnetic nasal dilator designed to open nasal passages and improve airflow. Rather than relying on a conventional adhesive strip stretched across the nose, its system uses adhesive tabs and a reusable magnetic band to pull the sides of the nose outward.

The organization markets its product to people looking to breathe more comfortably while sleeping, exercising or going about their daily routines. It indicates it has sold more than 100 million pairs of breathing tabs since 2023, with triple-digit revenue growth over the past three years.

Intake plans to use the latest capital to expand beyond its direct-to-consumer business and into more mainstream retail channels. That’s where Lubetzky’s experience building KIND into a household name could prove useful.

Industry observers note that its funding comes as venture investors show renewed enthusiasm for fitness and wellness. Startups in those categories raised more than $3.6 billion globally in the first half of 2026, putting the sector on pace for its strongest funding year since 2022, Crunchbase data highlights.

Interestingly, much of this year’s investment into the sector has flowed to wearable devices and health platforms built around AI and data. Intake is a somewhat different bet: a relatively simple physical product that has apparently found a sizable audience without promising to reinvent healthcare through software.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Fitness- And Wellness-Related Startup Funding In 2026.

Taking out the trash isn’t exactly rocket science. But managing the businesses that collect it turns out to be surprisingly complicated.

San Francisco-based TrashLab Software recently raised $12 million in a growth funding round led by Ventana, with participation from existing investors Bienville Capital, Harlem Capital and CreativeCo.

The startup builds an AI-powered operating platform for waste-hauling businesses, an industry where many smaller operators still rely on spreadsheets, paper routes and clunky software to manage their fleets.

In a recent development, trashLab notes its platform combines dispatching, route planning, customer management, billing and payments. Its AI agent, called Haul-E, can answer customer calls and take orders, while cameras in garbage trucks can help document problems such as overflowing dumpsters, blocked containers or bins that weren’t put out for collection.

Industry observers note that the company says hundreds of waste haulers across the U.S. and Canada now use its software, and that more than 5 million tons of material have been managed through its platform.

It’s not the only startup finding an AI opportunity in the waste industry. We recently covered Greyparrot, a London-based company using computer vision to identify and analyze waste moving through recycling facilities. While Greyparrot focuses on what happens after trash reaches a processing plant, TrashLab is tackling the messy logistics of getting it there.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Venture Funding To Waste Management Startups In 2026.

Factory automation has come a long way, but programming the machines that run industrial production lines can still require specialized expertise and a lot of time.

Gardena, California-based Neuron Industries wants to make the process a lot simpler.

The startup recently announced a $10 million seed round co-led by FCVC and Obvious Ventures, with participation from Y Combinator, Thin Line Capital, Zee Prime Capital and Founder Factor.

Neuron is developing a latest kind of industrial controller — the hardware that coordinates sensors, motors and other equipment in factories — alongside AI-powered software that lets engineers describe what they want a machine to do in ordinary language.

Its system generates control code that engineers can inspect, modify and test in simulation before deploying it to real equipment. The goal is to reduce the time and specialized programming knowledge needed to get upcoming production lines up and running.

The startup claims it has already demonstrated its technology on existing factory equipment, including replacing an aging controller on a wood-processing line with roughly three hours of engineering work and eight hours of downtime. It plans to release its Cortex AI Controller commercially in early 2027.

The investment fits into a broader surge in funding for physical AI — technology that applies artificial intelligence to robots, autonomous vehicles, industrial equipment and other machines in the real world. Startups in those categories raised $47.4 billion globally across 521 deals in the first half of 2026, nearly 4x the amount invested in the second half of 2025, according to Crunchbase data.

Related Crunchbase query: Global Physical AI Venture Funding In 2026.

Sending an experiment into space has traditionally required years of preparation, specialized engineering expertise and a very substantial budget.

Austria-based Tumbleweed wants to bring the cost of entry down to as little as 15,000 euros.

The Vienna startup recently raised 6.9 million euros (roughly $8 million) in seed funding led by PactVC, with participation from Vanagon Ventures, Prototype Capital and EWOR, among other investors. The firm describes it as the largest space-tech seed round raised in Austria to date.

Tumbleweed develops standardized containers, called Pods, that allow researchers and companies to conduct experiments in microgravity without building their own satellites or navigating the complex certification process required for space missions.

Recent findings suggest that customers can place their experiments inside the pre-certified containers, which provide power and communications capabilities while in orbit. The startup handles the logistics of launching the payloads and transmitting experimental data back to Earth.

Unlike many space startups still working toward their first launch, Tumbleweed has already put hardware in orbit. Its inaugural Oasis Alpha satellite launched in July carrying experiments for four paying customers, including research into biological processes and space-resource technologies. The mission was fully booked a year before launch.

Tumbleweed states its fresh funding will help it carry out three more missions in 2027 and develop a next-generation spacecraft that would allow customers to bring physical samples back to Earth beginning in 2028.

According to recent reports, tumbleweed is part of a growing European space startup ecosystem, although funding remains concentrated elsewhere. As of late August, European companies had attracted about 10% of global space-tech venture investment in 2026, compared with the more than 60% going to U.S. startups, Crunchbase data reveals.

Three months after introducing its product, AI cybersecurity startup Corma has raised a $125 million Series A round at a $1 billion valuation led by NEA, the company mentioned. Interest in its product skyrocketed after a series of security incidents sent chief information security officers scrambling on October 21 when a critical flaw was found in PHP, a popular web programming language. Popular open source tool LiteLLM, a proxy for routing requests to multiple LLM providers, also disclosed a security incident. Other incidents were disclosed that day, too. It has been revealed that corma isn’t the only company using AI to play defense. Other examples include Kevin Mandia’s upcoming startup Armadin, as well as Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, and other established players, and too many other startups to count. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Album VC, a Lehi, Utah-based early-stage venture firm that’s been known until now as Peak Ventures, just gathered up $75 million in capital commitments for its third early-stage fund.

The development shows investor confidence in Album’s young team, which came together in 2014 after the founder of Zinch — a site connecting colleges and students that sold to the ed-tech company Chegg in 2011 — decided to try his hand at investing in other startups.

As that founder, Sid Krommenhoek — who stayed on with Chegg for several years, running its international efforts — explains it, “I thought I’d do another startup. But I also knew from our own experience in struggling to raise money the need for more capital in Utah, and I thought having that operator-entrepreneur perspective could be useful.”.

Industry observers note that A first fund, like many in the industry, was more of an experiment, though it was a decent $23 million, thanks largely to the support of Chegg CEO Dan Rosensweig, who was early to commit capital to the fund. A second ($56 million) fund followed when Krommenhoek and John Mayfield — a friend who joined him from a marketing role at Qualtrics — began investing more seriously in their backyard and beyond.

In a recent development, they were soon joined by a third investor, Diogo Myrrha, who began as a principal with the firm and is now a general partner. Explains Krommenhoek of one of the many things that binds the three Brigham Young University grads, “We all came into Utah’s orbit when it wasn’t necessarily a place where you could live out your career, but that’s changed.”.

Breaking: Hank Green is self-funding ClockwiseTV, a curated educational video platform for kids

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“I was recently on a podcast and the host asked me what my lowest part of my career was,” Hank Green mused on a recent episode of his own podcast, Dear Hank & John.

That’s a tough question for anyone to answer, let alone someone who has spent about two decades regularly posting videos online for an increasingly broad audience.

“Really the low — the long low — was just watching as [the internet] went from being this lovely thing that a bunch of creatives were goofing around [on] to it being freaking everything, and mattering so much, and getting taken over by all tons of terrible vibes and algorithms selecting for outrage, and it being a huge degradation to the social order,” Green said.

That’s bleak, but Green is at least trying to lead by example in showing that we don’t have to accept that the good parts of the internet are gone forever. The notoriously entrepreneurial vlogbrother has spun up a fresh firm with Leslie Morgan: ClockwiseTV, a curated, ad-free educational video platform for children ages 8 to 12.

Sources indicate that “[Hank] came to me last September like, ‘I have had this idea for a really long time, and it stems from the fact that my child, who’s nine, always is asking me for five more minutes on whatever device he’s on,’” Morgan, who has spent 20 years working on the business side of the creator economy, told TechCrunch. “I was like, I have that same problem… ‘How do you contain time, but also give the child agency?’”.

Clockwise’s answer to that question seems to be this: At the start of each viewing session, the parent and child decide how long they can watch, and the platform will recommend videos that will adhere to that time frame. If a kid is in the midst of a 30-minute session and has already watched two 10-minute videos, they’re not going to be suggested a 20-minute video when they only have 10 minutes left.

According to recent reports, the startup is addressing a pretty widespread concern among parents, who are worried about more than simply negotiating with their children about how long they can use the iPad. According to a 2025 study by the Pew Research Center, about 51% of parents of children 12 or younger say their kid watches YouTube every day, among other video apps.

Sources indicate that youTube has a dedicated app for children under 13, YouTube Kids, which offers a wide range of parental controls, but the app can reportedly still serve children a wealth of low-quality AI slop. Other apps that don’t have a kids’ version can be even worse.

Clockwise says it is also solving that problem by hand-curating a library of educational videos from creators like Odd Animal Specimens, Draw with Jazza, and Nerdforge, as well as channels Green had a hand in creating, like Crash Course Kids and SciShow Kids.

“When you go into the app, there’s a dozen choices [of videos] that you can choose from to start,” Morgan, the startup’s CEO, mentioned. “There’s search functionality as well, so you can say, ‘Hey, I’m really interested in math today,’ so you can look up Stand-up Maths and look at what’s available in that time frame.”.

Some of these creators cater to people of all ages, but Clockwise states its team manually reviews each video it uploads and edits it so that it’s ready for younger eyes. The team might remove anything from embedded product placement to what Morgan calls “spectacle power tool use.”.

According to recent reports, “Simone Giertz, who’s a maker creator, tends to curse a lot. But a lot of that content is great for kids,” Morgan explains. “She makes a skateboard for her three-legged dog, and if she drops an f-bomb, we’re going to cut it out so that it’s suitable for children.”.

Sources indicate that clockwise pays these creators an upfront fee to use their videos, then shares 25% of revenue based on watch time. Clockwise charges parents $6.99 per month or $69.99 per year to access the platform, which it promises will remain free of ads.

“Humans are checking [the videos] four times at least before it’s ever published into our app […] That will always stay,” Morgan remarked. “We’re not interested in using AI to wash down our content.”.

So far, a few hundred parents have tested Clockwise with their children in beta. On Tuesday, the platform is opening to the public with apps made for iOS and Android smartphones and tablets.

The platform has not taken on any outside funding, and is funded by Green himself.

Recent findings suggest that “It was really important that he had full control,” Morgan said. “He wanted to invest his own wealth into this. That was also really important because it is something he just believes in so wholeheartedly, as do I.”.

Bitcoin (BTC), the world’s largest cryptocurrency, has recorded a multi-month high in daily trading volume as the cryptocurrency market remains in the grip of extreme volatility.

The massive spike in trading volume comes in the wake of one of the biggest sell-offs in BTC this year.

Recent findings suggest that on Nov. 21, the world’s largest cryptocurrency dropped as low as around $55,100, a level last seen in September 2024. Sources indicate that as per data from analytics firm CoinGlass, Bitcoin (BTC) futures trading volume stands at around $76.17 billion. On the other hand, the cryptocurrency's spot trading volume stands at $7.91 billion over the past 24 hours.

Despite the latest recovery, it is still trading 9.74% lower over the past seven days and more than 27% lower over the past month.

The world’s largest cryptocurrency is also down around 53.3% from its all-time high of $126,198.

Another massive wave of liquidations has swept through the cryptocurrency market following the latest recovery.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Science Corporation, the medical technology startup founded by former Neuralink president Max Hodak in 2021, raised a $400 million Series D, the firm said in a blog post.

Sources indicate that investors in the upcoming round valued the company at $3.5 billion, a person familiar with the deal told TechCrunch. Those backers included Khosla Ventures, the Ackman Oxman Institute, Tenet Healthcare, 885 Capital, Y Combinator, and PLC Neurotech.

Hodak, who talked his way into a graduate neuroscience lab as a college student and has pursued biotechnology ever since, co-founded Science to leverage latest technologies to understand and interact with the brain.

It has been revealed that science’s first product is PRIMA, a wearable and implantable chip that helps people with age-related macular degeneration recover some vision. The device is approved in Europe and available in Germany, as well as being trialed for new conditions.

Hodak confirmed that the device is now being trialed for patients with another blindness-causing condition, Stargardt disease, while onstage at TechCrunch Disrupt.

It has been revealed that with the funding, the tech giant aims to bring the device to the United States through the FDA’s Humanitarian Device Exemption, which lets experimental medical technology be used to treat rare conditions. Science has convinced the FDA that advanced macular degeneration in both eyes is uncommon enough to let them seek approval to use the device on people in the U.S.

Sources indicate that still, the startup’s big ambition and founding purpose is connecting directly to the human brain through a bio-hybrid sensor built from a combination of cultured neurons and silicon. The firm is currently designing initial human trials of the device with Yale neurosurgery professor Murat Günel, who told TechCrunch it could offer potential treatments for Parkinson’s disease, among other brain injuries and illnesses.

Bitcoin (BTC) bull and SkyBridge Capital founder Anthony Scaramucci has argued that the world's biggest cryptocurrency could find a critical bottom as soon as this week.

Scaramucci's comments follow the leading cryptocurrency's struggle to recover from a catastrophic crypto market crash that took BTC to its lowest price level in over two years.

Sources indicate that in the latest episode of All Things Markets on Nov. 20, the SkyBridge Capital founder joined Galaxy Digital CEO Mike Novogratz to discuss a potential bottom for Bitcoin.

According to recent reports, scaramucci shared his view that Bitcoin could see its bottom on Nov. 25, citing the cryptocurrency's four-year halving cycle as the driving force behind his comments.

"Before we came on, I asked ChatGPT when's the expected halving for Bitcoin," Scaramucci explained.

"And then when are we 500 days out from that halving? And the estimate was November 25th," he added.

This prediction stems from the idea that Bitcoin's price trends could follow a predictable four-year cycle that coincides with the cryptocurrency's halving events, when the new BTC supply is cut in half.

This theory suggests that Bitcoin could find its major bottom around the 500-day mark before its next halving, expected in 2028.

However, these theories are by no means a certainty when it comes to predicting future price action, especially with the current level of institutional participation and macroeconomic forces impacting the crypto market to an unprecedented extent.

During the conversation, Novogratz also took note of Bitcoin's history of forming double bottoms during its four-year cycles.

"And every four years, Bitcoin double bottomed," Novogratz remarked.

At the time, the Galaxy Digital CEO's comments suggested a potentially positive scenario, as Bitcoin had been able to hold its psychological $60,000 price level.

"If it doesn't break 60, that could be a good sign," he noted.

Unfortunately for Bitcoin, the cryptocurrency subsequently crashed below this critical price point. This has left some wondering whether the cryptocurrency has already found its ultimate bottom.

During the same conversation, Novogratz suggested that Bitcoin's short-term outlook could largely depend on the current situation in the stock market.

Specifically, the billionaire remarked that a rebound in tech stocks could lead to a strong rally in Bitcoin's price.

Sources indicate that "If we put in a bottom in the next couple days in the S&P here, down 3% from here, down 5% from here. And we have a rally back up. Man, Bitcoin is going to rally hard with it," Novogratz predicted.

However, he also warned that Bitcoin could see a lot of market-driven movements going forward, as opposed to crypto-specific movements.

"I think we're going to be stuck tethered to general sentiment and risk," he remarked.

Novogratz also believes that Bitcoin could trade in a range between $60,000 and $75,000 before a breakout or breakdown becomes apparent.

Industry observers note that bitcoin plunged to around $55,100 on Nov. 21, its lowest price level since September 2024, following another severe wave of sell-offs in the crypto market.

According to recent reports, it then bounced back strongly to climb above $60,000 again, albeit briefly, before falling back to around $59,000 on Nov. 22.
